Team Name: Smithtown Academy Bees 
Team Number: 17929 Challenge Category: Elementary 
 
 
How do different fertilizers combined with soil and moon regolith affect lettuce and radish growth? 
 
 
Background 
 
In the Spring 2024 Plant the Moon Challenge, we studied the affect of different soil supplements on the growth of 
both lettuce and radishes planted in 50/50 mixtures of soil and lunar simulant. We chose lettuce and radish plants 
because we wanted one plant growing above the soil and one below the soil. We evaluated bone meal, blood meal, 
and liquid kelp because they have different levels of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. 
 
Independent Variable 
 
The independent variable in this experiment is the soil supplement added to the 50/50 mixture of soil and lunar 
simulant. 
 
Dependent Variables 
 
The dependent variables included the number of sprouts in each pot, the height of the plant, the number of leaves 
per plant, and the circumference of the radishes. We also recorded the mass of each pot throughout the experiment 
but did not find that this changed significantly. 
 
Controls 
 
The control pots for the experiment included two pots of 100% soil and two pots of 50/50 soil and lunar regolith 
with no added supplements to either. Other controls included watering at the same amount and same timing for all 
plants. The water used was bottled water of the same brand throughout the experiment because our well water 
would have introduced other possible nutrients. All plants got the same lighting and same amount of lighting each 
day, which was approximately 12 hours per day, seven days per week. All seeds were planted at the same time and 
were kept in a make-shift greenhouse, where we wrapped heavy plastic around the table and lighting to keep the 
temperature warmer and humidity higher than the regular room temperature and humidity. All plants were 
measured and weighed at the same time and day, with measurements taken twice each week. All the experimental 
pots contained 50% soil and 50% lunar simulant. Each lettuce pot was planted with ten lettuce seeds, and each 
radish pot was planted with six radish seeds. All measurements used the same ruler and were taken by the same 
person throughout the experiment. The same scale was used for measuring weight as well. 
 
Project Hypothesis 
 
Our hypothesis was that the soil and moon regolith supplemented with bone meal would be the best for growing 
radishes because the higher phosphorus helps with root growth. We predicted the blood meal supplemented pots 
would be the best for lettuce because it has the most nitrogen and that is good for leaf growth. We thought the 
liquid kelp pots would be slightly better than the control pots because they had a little more nitrogen and even 
more potassium than the control soil and these help with overall growth. 
 
Experimental Design and Procedures 
 
We planted two control types for lettuce and two control types for radishes. The first control type was 100% soil 
and second control type was 50% soil with 50% lunar simulant. Then we planted pots of 50% moon regolith with 
50% soil that had bone meal added at the amount recommended on the packaging. The radish seeds had two of 
these pots and the lettuce had another two with the same mixture. Next, we planted pots of 50% moon regolith 
and 50% soil that had blood meal added at the amount recommended on the packaging. Again, the radish had two 
of these pot mixtures and the lettuce had another two. Last, we planted pots of 50% moon regolith and 50% soil,

and liquid kelp was added to water in a spray bottle at the recommended quantity. This water mixture was kept 
separate from the plain bottled water and the liquid kelp supplemented water was used on these pots each time 
they were watered. The water was only stored in a spray bottle to keep it separate and the water was poured on the 
pots like we did with all the other plants. All other pots were watered with plain bottled water with no added 
fertilizer. We used bottled water because we have well water, and it can add other nutrients not expected in our 
experiment. At the end of the fourth week, we also gave another dose of bone meal and blood meal supplement to 
those pots because the packaging had recommended once a month fertilizing. 
 
Planting took place on February 5, 2024. Lettuce and radish seeds were planted in different pots with each of the 
mixtures described. We planted ten lettuce seeds at a ¼ inch depth in each lettuce pot and six radish seeds at a ½ 
inch depth in each radish pot. The soil mixtures were planted with a seed starter peat pot that was cut in half and 
placed near the bottom of the 4-inch plastic container. We did this because we had read on the Plant the Moon 
website that the moon regolith dried out quickly, and we thought this would help keep moisture in the soil. During 
the first month of growing, we also aerated the soil once a week using a small wooden food skewer to poke two 
holes in the soil of each pot prior to watering. We did this because we had read that the moon regolith became 
clay-like when watered, and we thought this would help get oxygen to the roots better. 
 
We planned to thin the plants to the biggest growing sprout after a week of above ground growth. When sprouts 
began to appear at days four and five, we decided to cover each pot with plastic wrap held in place with a 
rubberband. This was kept on the pot to help keep the soil moist because we were concerned about the 
evaporation happening and the soil becoming too dry. The plastic wrap was left on until the sprout was touching 
it. We waited until February 26, 2024 to thin the radish plants and February 27, 2024 to thin the lettuce plants. We 
hesitated on thinning because we were concerned we would have die off afterwards. Rather than thinning to one 
plant per pot, as we had originally planned, we decided to keep two plants per pot after we learned that radishes 
grown in pots indoors could be thinned to an inch apart and still grow well. We thinned the lettuce also to two 
sprouts per pot, except one pot which only had one sprout germinate (L3B). We did not believe that two sprouts 
would greatly affect one another in growing and this would help protect against complete loss by die off if it 
occurred in the pots once they were thinned. 
 
All pots were placed under the grow lights for approximately 12-hour light periods each day and 12-hour dark 
periods. We looked up the watering needs of radishes and lettuce at the Iowa State Extension website and found 
that each vegetable needed about an inch of water per week to grow. An inch of water is about 25 mL so we 
watered twice a week. We measured the soil moisture and determined that twice a week watering would be 
needed to keep the soil adequately moist. All plants were watered approximately 24 hours before they were 
weighed and measured, so watering was done on Mondays and Thursdays. 
 
The lettuce and radish pots were each labeled to indicate which ones were controls and which were each of the 
three treatments. For example, lettuce had L1A & L1B = control with 100% soil; L2A & L2B = control with 50% 
simulant and 50% soil; L3A & L3B = 50% simulant and 50% soil with bone meal; L4A & L4B = 50% simulant 
and 50% soil with blood meal; and L5A & L5B = 50% simulant and 50% soil which was watered with liquid kelp 
mixture. We did the same kind of number system for the radishes (R1A, R1B; R2A, R2B; R3A, R3B; R4A, R4B; 
R5A, R5B). 
 
Measurements were recorded twice each week on Tuesdays and Fridays. All pots were weighed after all the soil 
and/or simulant were potted, along with a full watering in the 24 hours before the grow period started. The seeds 
were added on the first day of the growing period (February 5, 2024) and an initial weight was recorded to track 
the percent of weight change for each pot. Pots were weighed once per week on Fridays throughout the 
experiment. We counted the number of sprouts for each pot and recorded this number. For lettuce, we counted the 
number of cotyledons and leaves of each plant and recorded these twice each week. The height for the tallest plant 
in each lettuce pot was recorded at each measurement. For the radishes, we counted the number of cotyledons and 
leaves twice each week. The height of the tallest plant in each radish pot was recorded at each measurement. 
When we harvested, we also measured the circumference of any radish growth. The counting of cotyledons and 
leaves began at the end of the fifth week of growing since this is when they first became distinct.

Results 
 
Looking at the percentages of successful germination, the 100% soil control and the 50/50 soil and lunar simulant 
with blood meal both had 100% average germination in the radish pots. The radish pots with 50/50 soil and 
regolith with no fertilizer and the pots with liquid kelp added both had average germination of 75%. The 50/50 
soil and regolith treated with bone meal had the lowest average germination at 58%. 
 
With the lettuce plants, the best average germination was in the 50/50 soil and regolith treated with liquid kelp. 
They had an 85% germination rate. The 100% soil control had an 80% germination success. The 50/50 soil and 
lunar simulant with no fertilizer had a 75% germination rate. One of the lower germination rates was in the 50/50 
soil and regolith with blood meal, and it had a 45% germination rate. The lowest germination rate was in the 
50/50 soil and regolith with bone meal, and it had only a 35% germination rate. 
 
For the radish plants, the best grower in terms of height was R4A, which was the 50/50 soil and regolith treated 
with blood meal. It was consistently the tallest plant and ended up being 12.4 cm tall. The second tallest plant was 
in the other 50/50 soil and regolith pot treated with blood meal (R4B). It was 11.5 cm tall. When the radishes were 
harvested on March 31, 2024, the R4A plant was the plant that grew a 3.5 cm in circumference radish. 
Surprisingly, the R4B did not have any radish growth. The R3A plant, which was the 50/50 soil and regolith with 
bone meal, had the only other radish growth with a 1.5 cm circumference radish even though this plant only grew 
to 7.2 cm. The liquid kelp treated plant did well initially in growing but then stopped making good progress about 
half way through the growing cycle. The 100% soil control radish plant was the second largest growing initially. 
About halfway into the growing cycle, it moved back to the third place in growing and then stopped growing. But 
it did not produce any radish growth. (See table 1.) 
 
In looking at the growth in the height of the greens for the lettuce, the L4A plant, which was a 50/50 soil and 
regolith treated with blood meal, did the best most consistently. It ended up being 9.9 cm in height and had the 
most leaves with six in all. The second best growth in height was the L3B lettuce plant, which was a 50/50 soil 
and regolith treated with bone meal. This plant grew to be 6.7 cm in height and had five total leaves. It is 
important to note that this pot had only one plant in it due to only one seed germinating. This could have affected 
its growth in a positive way. The L5A and L5B plants, which were treated with liquid kelp, were good growers in 
the first month but then stopped growing much. During the second month of growing, the L4B plant, which was 
treated with blood meal, consistently was the third highest grower and ended at 5.3 cm and four leaves. (See table 
2.) 
 
While we measured the mass of the pots throughout the experiment, it was not very helpful information because 
there was not enough significant growth to change the weight much. (See figures 1 and 2.) 
 
 
Conclusion 
 
Our hypothesis was that the soil and moon regolith supplemented with bone meal would be the best for growing 
radishes because the higher phosphorus helps with root growth. We did not find this hypothesis to be correct. We 
also thought that the blood meal supplemented pots would be best for lettuce because it had the most nitrogen and 
that is good for leaf growth. This hypothesis was correct. The lettuce plants in the 50/50 soil and lunar simulant 
with blood meal grew the best in height and number of leaves. Interestingly, the same results happened for the 
radish plants in the 50/50 soil and regolith with blood meal. These radish plants grew the tallest and one of them 
produced the largest of two radishes at harvest. We think the bigger leaves and taller plant helped bring in more 
nutrients from the grow lights to help produce a radish. Also, we saw a good growth spurt in both lettuce and 
radish plants after the second dose of blood meal supplement at the end of week four. (See figures 3 and 4.) Our 
last hypothesis was that the liquid kelp pots would be slightly better than the control pots (either 100% soil or the 
50/50 soil and regolith with no fertilizer) because liquid kelp has more nitrogen and even more potassium than 
these controls and would help with overall growth. This hypothesis was partially correct because it helped with 
growth in the beginning but did not result in significantly bigger or better plant growth.

For germination, we wonder if liquid kelp would help for starting the plants in growing. We saw that the plants 
treated with liquid kelp had some of the better germination and better initial growing. This did not seem to help 
after the first month of growing though. 
 
For a follow up experiment, we would recommend using liquid kelp supplement to get the plants started and then 
to switch to blood meal to help with leaf growth. We think this will produce larger lettuce and radish plants and 
maybe more successful radish growth. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
References 
 
Iowa State University Extension and Outreach: Horticulture and Home Pest News. (2022, May). Growing Leafy 
Greens in Iowa. hortnews.extension.iastate.edu/growing-leafy-greens-iowa 
 
Steil, A. (2023, April). Growing Radishes in Iowa. Iowa State University Extension and Outreach: Horticulture 
and Home Pest News. hortnews.extension.iastate.edu/growing-radishes-iowa
